chaturanga-manasollasa.title: Digital Ludeme Project · Manasollasa evidence record
chaturanga-manasollasa.supports: Twelfth-century four-handed rules evidence dated 1126–1138, not a sixth-century record.

chaturanga-roots.supports: Indian origins of chaturanga and four army divisions; does not establish exact 574 CE.

xiangqi-wxf.supports: Current form no later than Song; older royal-origin theories; river, intersections and cannon mechanics.

shogi-japan.title: Japan Shogi Association · Japanese Shogi History (1)
shogi-japan.supports: Pieces with 1058 tablet, 15th–16th-century modern form and captured-piece reuse.

shogi-rules.supports: 9×9 board, twenty pieces per player, movement, promotion and drops.

sanyou-bibliography.title: San You Qi Pu · bibliographic entry
sanyou-bibliography.supports: Zheng Jinde attribution and Kangxi / Daoguang Zhaodai Congshu editions; primary page scan not inspected.

yanyi-patent.supports: Filed 22 August 2005, published 21 February 2007; 53 pieces; separate Han force and alliance rules.

cognition-rct.supports: No statistically significant mathematical/metacognitive advantage; no basis for stronger claims about app games.

cognition-eef.supports: No detected mathematics, reading or science attainment benefit in tested program.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Four armies. One frozen meeting place.
screens.text: The name chaturanga evokes four divisions of an army: infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots. Here, their story meets an Antarctic celebration.
screens.scene: Four existing armies rise gently into view; the host stands beside the board.

screens.label: Documented history · later four-player evidence
screens.title: Royal dice across the centuries.
screens.text: Around 1030, the scholar al-Biruni described a game of four-person chess played with dice in India. Our icy court celebrates the imaginative possibilities of this remarkable chess family.
screens.scene: Long dice turn beside an illustrated manuscript; no actual historical king or portrait.
screens.historicalNote: Around 1030, al-Biruni described four people playing chess with dice. That record is later than chaturanga’s early Indian roots; it does not date these rules to 574 CE.

screens.label: Your edition · modern adaptation
screens.title: Let the roll open your choices.
screens.text: Our four-player dice and 2v2 edition adapts this wider family. Follow the legal-move guide, learn one piece at a time, or head straight to your table.
screens.scene: Highlight current piece roles and the existing game guide; do not change movement from this story.

xiangqi.title: Xiangqi
xiangqi.origin: China · present form by the Song dynasty

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: A river divides the board.
screens.text: The armies meet on intersections, with a river between them and a palace at each end. Watch the cannon: it captures by jumping exactly one intervening piece.
screens.scene: Cannon and chariot glide over the existing board, outside live play.

screens.label: Documented history · origin theories distinguished
screens.title: A royal game through the dynasties.
screens.text: The World Xiangqi Federation traces the form of today's game to at least the Song dynasty (960–1279). Generations of players have explored its palace, river and decisive cannon tactics.
screens.scene: Pengu opens a Song-era inspired map; label artwork as interpretation.
screens.historicalNote: The World Xiangqi Federation places the present form no later than the Song dynasty, 960–1279. Stories crediting ancient rulers or generals remain origin theories.

screens.label: Your table · rules first
screens.title: Read the lines before the battle.
screens.text: Start with the river, palace and blocked horse leg. Your movement lesson shows the legal destinations; practice first or take your seat.
screens.scene: Use current native symbols and existing legal-move overlays.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: A captured piece can return on your side.
screens.text: In shogi, a capture can give you a future move: an unpromoted piece may re-enter under your command. The board keeps changing even as pieces leave it.
screens.scene: A captured native tile rests by the board, then returns on a legal demonstration square.

screens.label: Documented history
screens.title: A treasure from Nara, dated 1058.
screens.text: At Kōfukuji in Nara, shogi pieces were found beside a wooden tablet dated 1058. Over the centuries, the game developed its extraordinary way of returning captured pieces to the battlefield.
screens.scene: Pengu lifts an illustrated date card; no copied museum image.
screens.historicalNote: At Kōfukuji in Nara, shogi pieces were found with a wooden tablet dated 1058. The modern game developed later, including the distinctive reuse of captured pieces.

screens.label: Your table · living tradition
screens.title: Promotion changes the next chapter.
screens.text: Explore the 9×9 board, promotion and drops. The guide explains the limits as well as the possibilities, so your first return to the board is a legal one.
screens.scene: Show native front/back tile roles and a legal drop example from the current engine.

sannin.title: Sannin Shogi
sannin.edition: Selected Kokusai Sannin Shogi digital rules

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Now the third army takes its seat.
screens.text: Three commanders share one hexagonal battlefield. Your next decision has two audiences: the rival you approach, and the rival watching you.
screens.scene: Three existing armies appear in sequence; host outside the playing area.

screens.label: Documented history · twentieth-century design
screens.title: A newspaper could carry an entire game.
screens.text: Tokyo’s museum collection records a Kokusai Sannin Shogi board issued with the 1 January 1933 Hinode magazine. Sanko Library also lists a 1932 rulebook.
screens.scene: An original illustrated magazine folds open to the game, without reproducing the historic printed artwork.

screens.label: Your edition · selected rules
screens.title: Find your place on the three-sided board.
screens.text: This inventive three-player shogi design emerged in Japan in the 1930s. Discover its hexagonal paths, shifting alliances and the tactics of three commanders.
screens.scene: Current 127-cell board with native piece labels and the existing central target.
screens.historicalNote: This is a historical shogi variant, not an ancient Japanese game. Let the movement lesson orient you before you explore alliances and the centre of the current digital board.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Three kingdoms change every calculation.
screens.text: Wei, Shu and Wu face one another across a shared battlefield. A move against one rival can open an opportunity for the other.
screens.scene: Existing three armies animate a short noninteractive greeting.

screens.label: Historical context · reconstruction boundary
screens.title: Three kingdoms, one enduring challenge.
screens.text: Three-player Xiangqi designs appear in China's late-imperial board-game traditions. The stories of Wei, Shu and Wu offer a vivid setting for a contest in which every alliance shapes the next move.
screens.scene: Use three banners and an illustrated archive; do not depict ancient rulers as verified players.
screens.historicalNote: Three-player Xiangqi designs have a documented late-imperial history. The Three Kingdoms theme does not prove the game was played in that ancient period. Exact rules and dating vary between designs.

screens.label: Your edition · digital reconstruction
screens.title: Read this board’s own rulebook.
screens.text: This app uses its selected three-sector rules and completion rules. Learn its routes, army transfers and victory conditions before assuming a familiar Xiangqi move works the same way.
screens.scene: Inspect the current topology and transfer guides without importing Yan Yi rules.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Three friends. Terrain with a say.
screens.text: Mountains, a sea and city walls change how armies meet. Flag and Fire join the familiar Xiangqi family: two small names with very different possibilities.
screens.scene: Native Flag and Fire roles approach the supplied terrain board.

screens.label: Documented tradition · evidence boundary
screens.title: An extraordinary chess family.
screens.text: Research places Three Friends Chess in seventeenth-century China, with eighteen pieces on each side. Fire, Flag and mountain routes make this a fascinating branch of the Xiangqi family.
screens.scene: An illustrated manual and three coloured seals; no claim of exact invention year.
screens.historicalNote: Research places Three Friends Chess in late-seventeenth-century China, with eighteen pieces per player. Bibliographic records attribute its manual to Zheng Jinde; the original page scan remains to be checked.

screens.label: Your edition · reconstruction
screens.title: Follow the lines of this edition.
screens.text: The exact 156 intersections, central routes and terrain boundaries belong to this digital reconstruction. The board lesson teaches those paths directly.
screens.scene: Show the existing fixed graph and current guide, preserving all coordinates.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: The quiet fourth force matters.
screens.text: Three players command Wei, Shu and Wu. The separate Han force waits at the edge of the contest, turning alliance decisions into a new kind of pressure.
screens.scene: The three armies greet the player while the yellow Han force remains distinct.

screens.label: Documented modern design
screens.title: Three kingdoms, a fresh invention.
screens.text: The designer Zhai Hui filed this inventive Three Kingdoms game in 2005. Its 2007 publication reveals a clever new chess design with a separate Han imperial force.
screens.scene: A date stamp sits next to an illustrated design sheet.
screens.historicalNote: Zhai Hui’s design was filed on 22 August 2005 and published in 2007. Its Three Kingdoms setting is inspiration, not the date of invention.

screens.label: Your table · chosen rule profile
screens.title: Five pieces can change the balance.
screens.text: The design specifies a Han emperor, three chariots and one cannon. Learn the alliance and control rules of this edition before stepping onto its special points.
screens.scene: Keep the emperor yellow and separate from the three human player identities.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Land, air and sea share the plan.
screens.text: Commander Chess brings different unit roles onto one terrain board. Watch how their movement, transport and protection fit together before launching an operation.
screens.scene: Animate existing native unit icons as a gentle assembly, without violence.

screens.label: Documented modern origin
screens.title: A modern Vietnamese creation.
screens.text: Writer and colonel Nguyễn Quý Hải created Commander Chess, an original Vietnamese strategy game whose copyright recognition was recorded on 16 November 2010. Its combined forces reward careful coordination.
screens.scene: A respectful illustrated writing desk and Vietnam-inspired coastal map.
screens.historicalNote: Vietnam’s sports authority identifies writer and colonel Nguyễn Quý Hải as the creator, with official copyright recognition on 16 November 2010. This is a modern Vietnamese game.

screens.label: Your edition · research status
screens.title: Begin at the practice table.
screens.text: This app’s selected reconstruction is under rules review. Use the unit guide and practice modes; check the stated rules profile rather than treating Antarctic artwork as original Vietnamese pieces.
screens.scene: Clearly retain the practice/review status and source-native unit labels.

screens.label: Cinematic welcome · artistic interpretation
screens.title: Mountains and rivers divide the task.
screens.text: Four corner armies share the landscape. Two infantry roles answer different boundaries, and diagonal allies must work together across the board.
screens.scene: Existing board terrain unfolds without changing its thirteen-by-thirteen geometry.

screens.label: Creator-associated source · unresolved dating
screens.title: The chess of mountains and rivers.
screens.text: A 2024 rules demonstration by 棋行山水 introduces a dramatic landscape game where four armies navigate rivers, mountains and shifting routes.
screens.scene: An illustrated source card marked 2024 explanation, not 2024 invention.
screens.historicalNote: Our reference is a 2024 basic-rules explanation by 棋行山水. Its invention date and full creator rulebook remain unverified; this particular adaptation is not presented as ancient.

screens.label: Your edition · explicit adaptation
screens.title: Choose two commanders or four.
screens.text: The source format gives each of two players two armies. This edition also offers four-player 2v2, labelled as an Antarctic adaptation. Learn the terrain before your first crossing.
screens.scene: Display the current two-seat and four-seat modes with fixed diagonal allies.
